Every Block, Once

This page shows every block and every figure kind a page can use, each one once, as it looks on a finished page. Open it beside a page template when you choose how to show a piece of content.

Writing a page takes two files: the page template for the kind you are writing, which carries its masthead and its sections, and this page, which carries what every kind shares. Open both. This is a reference you consult, never a file you copy — and it is an HTML vocabulary: a markdown seat file keeps markdown's own components, and the renderer gives each one the form you see here.

Normal content — no block, and no ceremony

Most of a page is this: paragraphs, lists, numbered steps and subheadings, written plainly and marked as nothing at all. A block is not how you write a section. It is what you drop into the writing when something must not read as prose. So start here, and reach for a block only when the content has a shape of its own.

Words — blocks that set writing apart

Each one below is a block: it carries a border, a background or a form of its own, so a reader sees it is not the surrounding prose before reading a word of it. Use one when the content is a rule, a set, a comparison, a literal, a shape, or a passage that belongs in its own panel.

PROSE — the markdown block

{{A passage that explains. Use it wherever the content is plain writing and no other block fits: REASONS is for prose that makes a claim and gives grounds, and this is for prose that simply teaches. It carries its own border, background and text colour, so it reads as a block the page chose rather than as the page's own voice continuing. Everything markdown gives you renders inside it.}}

CODE — one block per language the shared script colours

{{Tag every block with its language, as data-lang on the pre. The file holds plain code. The shared script, sds-docs.js, reads the tag when the page opens and colours the block, so nobody writes a colour into a page. A block with no tag is never coloured.}}

ts — a contract as it is declared, a comment per member

export interface SPRepo {
  type: SPRepoType;   // the world, and the whole of what a tool dispatches on
  name: CDTString;          // what a person calls this repository
  config: SPRepoConfig | null;
}

json — a manifest, with real values

{
  "type": "APPS",
  "name": "Platform",
  "config": { "stack": "TS", "deploys": true, "platform": null }
}

yaml — a declaration a person edits

# one environment row, as the estate declares it
setup: dev
region: in
deploy:
  mtype: BRANCH
  branch: develop

sql — the authoritative shape of a table

CREATE TABLE iam_identity (
  id CHAR(26) PRIMARY KEY,
  handle VARCHAR(180) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

sh — a command somebody else can run

# bring a repository to the standard, then wire its agent
spnutils repo create platform
spnutils repo agent-sync

md — markdown shown as source, when the page is about the markup

MAP — the parts of one thing

{{What you are looking at: the whole, then its parts and what flows between them.}}

SEQUENCE figure — who speaks to whom

{{What you are looking at: the participants, and the order they speak in. Use this instead of a flow whenever more than one party acts and who acted is the thing to see.}}

ENTITIES figure — what relates to what

SYSTEM — the architecture of a thing you build

{{What you are looking at: one bounded thing, its layers in the direction a call travels, and what it talks to outside its boundary. Use it for a server module, a web module, an app or an estate package — they are the same picture, and drawing them alike is the point.}}

The three rules

One outermost container, and it is the thing being described. Anything outside it is something the thing talks to, so a reader sees what is yours before reading a label. Inside it, boxes are grouped into layers that run one way — the direction a call travels — so the direction is learned once and never again. An edge is a call or data, and it carries what flows; an unlabelled line meaning related is the one thing this kind refuses.

It is a MAP with those three rules added, so the drawer is unchanged. MAP keeps its own job: the parts of one thing, where there is no inside and no order.

a server module — read the layers from the bottom: config, the environment it is started with, then app, then entry. Each door is met by the thing that knocks on it, and services and repositories are what reach outside

a web module — the same skeleton, drawn to the same coordinates as the server above. Read it from the bottom too: config, then app, then entry

an estate package — the same skeleton again. Here the layers are containment rather than call order, and it still reads from the bottom: what is declared, then what runs, then what is reachable

FLOWCHART — a path somebody takes, in the shapes a flowchart has

{{What you are looking at: where the path starts, each step, and the points where it branches. Use this rather than a MAP whenever the content is a path rather than a set of parts — a MAP answers what is this made of, a flowchart answers what happens, and where does it turn. The shape carries the meaning, so a reader reads the picture before the labels.}}

ShapeMeansDrawn as
Terminatorwhere the path starts, and where it endsa rectangle with fully rounded ends
Processone step: something is donea plain rectangle
Decisionthe path branches, and each branch carries its answera diamond
Input or outputsomething is read in or handed backa parallelogram
Predefined processa step defined somewhere else — a routine, a command, another flowa rectangle with a bar down each side
Data storesomething is read from or written to a storea cylinder
On-page connectorthe path continues from the matching letter, where a line would cross the pagea small circle with a letter in it

MAP figure, at its hardest — a cloud estate

{{What you are looking at: the accounts an organization holds, then one of them opened up. This is still a MAP — containers holding boxes — and it holds the nesting rule: the account holds the network, the network holds the subnets, and nothing goes deeper. A third level is the first thing you will want and the first thing to cut.}}

SKELETON — a mock of a layout

{{What you are looking at: the thing’s outer frame, and where each of its places sits.}} A skeleton is a preview: each place reads by its own mark, never by a tint — a dotted boundary with a name for a component, a part or a slot; a background for raised, a solid line for bordered, neither for flat — in plain words or by a block’s prop where one exists, and nothing shows the library’s look. A construct page or an overview asks for one in a dg block of kind skeleton; a hand-written page takes the drawing from docs figure draw <spec>. One sample at each level:

A page — a listing page: the layout’s places around a container whose content is the data table.

A layout — the RAIL layout: its five named places, each one block with its name.

A container — a container’s parts in their one order: its header above its outline, then its content and its footer inside it.

The looks of a container — the same three parts, eight ways: which parts share a frame, and whether that frame is raised, bordered and rounded.

A widget — the data table: its bar, its records with a head band and sample values, and its pagination.

A component — a dialog, one of the few components that frame others, over its scrim.

A showcase section — one block’s section: its example, its code open with Copy, its variants, states, props and links.

The same skeleton also draws a page as a person sees it, from sample values. A container has its title and its actions above a thin rounded outline; a card is a smaller outline with its title inside; a line of a list is an item with its facts under its title; and a field is the library’s form field or its data unit. A part with no border of its own, such as the header of a container or a row of the page beside its containers, may be marked by a dotted line with marked, where a figure is about the parts and what they line up with. A figure that shows a page for its content leaves it off, as these five do:

A page as a person sees it — a listing: one container, with its title and its main action above its outline, its filter bar, its records with no room around them, and its paging in its footer. One view for each screen class.

A form — a large form is one container: its sections are the parts of its content, each with its own title, and its actions stand in its footer.

A field that is read, beside one that is entered — a reading is its title with its value under it, as the library’s data unit shows it.

A record and its lists — the record is the header of the page: its picture in a circle, its name, and its facts on the line under the name. Each list attached to it is a container.

A value changed in a table — a row is read until a person opens it, and then its cell is a box as wide as the cell, with the action that saves it beside the box.

Colour and layout — tones, statuses and utilities

{{The classes a block or a drawing takes for its colour, and the utilities for a layout no block covers.}}

PALETTE — the tones a drawing, a chart or a badge may take

Put one tone class on a box, a connector, an arrowhead or a badge. A tone is a plain colour for a drawing or a chart, and it carries no meaning. A tone is a pair of tokens, so both themes follow, and a page never writes a colour of its own. A chart takes its series starting at violet, cyan, pink and olive, so a red line is not read as an error. To say how a thing stands, use a status class, shown in the next block.

STATUS — info, success, warning and error

A status says how a thing stands. Put one status class on a badge or a pull. Each status has two tokens of its own, the colour and its soft ground, and each has a dark value: --sds-info and --sds-info-soft, and so on. A status is never a tone of the palette, so changing a warning does not change a chart.

ClassOn a badgeUse it when
sds-infoinfothe reader should know something, and nothing is wrong
sds-successsuccessa thing is done, proven or allowed
sds-warningwarninga thing has a gap, or needs care
sds-errorerrora thing failed, was refused or was removed
Info

A pull that carries sds-info: something the reader should know.

Success

A pull that carries sds-success: the step ran, and the check passed.

Warning

A pull that carries sds-warning: this works, and one part of it is still done by hand.

Error

A pull that carries sds-error: the command stopped, and nothing was written.

A pull may hold a heading and a table in place of a label and a paragraph. The heading is an h4, and a badge may sit beside its words. A row's th names what its td says. The pull below carries sds-warning, and a hub writes a declared gap in this form.

UTILITIES — a layout that no block covers

Use a named class first. Use a Tailwind utility only for a layout that no block covers. A utility reads the same tokens as a named class, so both themes follow. Below, utilities put two boxes in one row. The first box is the named class sds-pull. The second box has no class of ours, and every part of its look is a utility.

A named class

sds-pull m-0 — the block, and one utility that takes away its margin inside the row.

Utilities alone

border border-ok bg-ok-soft rounded-sm px-5 py-4 — the same tokens, read through Tailwind.

The built stylesheet holds one standard set of utilities, and no other utility has a rule in it. The chapter lists the set by family. The row below uses three of them: flex and justify-between put its two ends apart, and text-faint writes the second end in faint text.
